subject: Mathematics
source: Drive: Maths folder (SoW Maths, Secondary National Curriculum Mathematics, GCSE Maths folder); Edexcel GCSE Mathematics (1MA1) specification

lessons.title: Expanding double brackets
objectives: Expand and simplify two linear brackets
Expand squared brackets such as (x + 4)²
Recognise the difference of two squares

keywords.def: an expression whose highest power of x is x²
multiply out brackets and simplify
an expression of the form a² − b², which equals (a + b)(a − b)

teach.heading: The grid method
bullets: Multiply each term in the first bracket by each in the second.
teach.note: Draw a 2 by 2 grid with x and 3 across the top and x and 5 down the side. The four boxes are x², 5x, 3x and 15. Check by substituting x = 1: 4 × 6 = 24 and 1 + 8 + 15 = 24 ✓.

teach.heading: Negative terms
bullets: Keep the sign with each term.
teach.note: Pupils make the most errors with signs. Write −2 in the grid, not 2. Check with x = 1: (−1)(8) = −8 and 1 + 5 − 14 = −8 ✓.

teach.heading: Coefficients in front of x
teach.note: Four terms are always produced; then collect like terms. Ask: which two terms combine? (−8x and +x.) FOIL (first, outer, inner, last) is a mnemonic, but the grid is more reliable.

teach.heading: Squared brackets
teach.note: Misconception: (x + 4)² = x² + 16. Expand it fully to show the middle term 8x. Use a geometric square of side x + 4 divided into x², two 4x rectangles and a 4 by 4 square.

teach.heading: Difference of two squares
teach.note: Expand it: x² − 6x + 6x − 36. Ask pupils to predict (x + 9)(x − 9) before expanding (x² − 81). This is used again when factorising. Link: 51² − 49² = 100 × 2 = 200 quickly.

practice: Expand and simplify (x + 2)(x + 9).
Expand and simplify (x − 3)(x − 8).
Expand and simplify (3x + 2)(x − 5).
independent: Expand (x + 5)(x − 4) and (2x − 1)(x + 6).
Expand (2x − 3)² and (x + 7)².
Expand (x + 8)(x − 8) and (3x + 2)(3x − 2).
exit: Expand and simplify (x + 6)(x − 2).
Expand (x − 3)².
lessons.homework: Complete eight double-bracket expansions and check each by substituting x = 2.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-drawn grids and colour-coded signs. Stretch: expand (x + 2)(x + 3)(x − 1).

lessons.title: Factorising quadratic expressions
objectives: Factorise x² + bx + c into two brackets
Factorise the difference of two squares
Factorise ax² + bx + c where a is greater than 1

keywords.def: write an expression as a product of brackets
the result of adding numbers
the result of multiplying numbers

starter: Find two numbers with sum 7 and product 12.

teach.heading: x² + bx + c
bullets: Find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.
teach.note: Always list factor pairs of c. Check by expanding. Ask: why must both numbers be positive when b and c are both positive? Because they add and multiply to positive values.

teach.heading: Negative numbers
teach.note: If c is negative, the numbers have different signs. Factor pairs of 24: 1 and 24, 2 and 12, 3 and 8, 4 and 6. Which pair differs by 2? 4 and 6, with the larger positive. Check: 6 × (−4) = −24 and 6 − 4 = 2 ✓.

teach.heading: Both negative
teach.note: If c is positive and b is negative, both numbers are negative. Quick check: expand (x − 4)(x − 5) = x² − 5x − 4x + 20 ✓.

teach.heading: Difference of two squares
bullets: x² + 5x = x(x + 5) is a common factor.
Always look for a common factor first.
teach.note: There is no x term in x² − 49, so the two numbers add to 0: +7 and −7. Remind pupils that x² + 49 cannot be factorised. Practise spotting the type of expression before starting.

teach.heading: Harder: ax² + bx + c (Higher)
bullets: 2x² + 7x + 3: find two numbers with product 6 and sum 7.
teach.note: Multiply a × c = 6, find the pair with sum 7 (6 and 1), split the middle term, then factorise in pairs. Check by expanding: 2x² + 6x + x + 3 ✓. This is Higher tier content; Foundation pupils continue with x² + bx + c.

practice: Factorise x² + 7x + 12.
Factorise x² − x − 12.
Factorise x² − 81.
independent: Factorise x² + 10x + 21, x² − 3x − 10 and x² − 11x + 28.
Factorise x² − 100 and 4x² − 25.
Higher: factorise 3x² + 10x + 8.
exit: Factorise x² + 5x + 6.
Factorise x² − 16.
lessons.homework: Factorise eight quadratics and check every answer by expanding.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: factor pair tables and a sum-and-product grid. Stretch: factorise 6x² − x − 2.

lessons.title: Solving quadratic equations by factorising
objectives: Solve quadratic equations by factorising
Rearrange to equal zero first
Use quadratic equations to solve area problems

keywords.def: an equation that can be written as ax² + bx + c = 0
a solution of an equation
if two factors multiply to zero, at least one factor is zero

starter: If a × b = 0, what can you say about a and b?

teach.heading: The null factor law
teach.note: This is why the equation must equal zero. Ask: could (x + 2)(x + 3) = 12 be solved by setting each bracket to 12? No. Check each solution by substituting: (−2 + 2)(−2 + 3) = 0 ✓.

teach.heading: Factorise then solve
teach.note: Show the full format: equation = 0, factorise, split into two linear equations, state both answers. Two answers are expected, unless the quadratic is a perfect square (x + 3)² = 0 which gives one repeated root.

teach.heading: Missing terms
teach.note: Never divide both sides by x, since that loses the solution x = 0. For x² = 16 write x = ±4. Ask: how do we write two answers together? ±4.

teach.heading: Rearrange first
teach.note: Collect everything on one side so the other is zero, with x² positive. Check: x = 5: 25 = 15 + 10 ✓. x = −2: 4 = −6 + 10 ✓.

teach.heading: Area problem
bullets: Rectangle: length x + 3, width x, area 40.
teach.note: Reject x = −8 because lengths are positive. Check: width 5, length 8, area 40 ✓. Higher: 2x² + 7x + 3 = 0 factorises as (2x + 1)(x + 3) = 0 giving x = −1/2 or x = −3.

practice: Solve x² + 7x + 12 = 0.
Solve x² − 9x = 0.
Solve x² − 25 = 0.
independent: Solve x² − 2x − 15 = 0 and x² + 4x = 21.
Solve x² = 5x − 6.
A rectangle has length x + 5 and width x. Its area is 24. Find x.
exit: Solve x² + 3x − 10 = 0.
Solve x² − 36 = 0.
lessons.homework: Solve six quadratics by factorising, checking each answer by substitution.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: step-by-step solution frames. Stretch: solve 6x² − 5x − 6 = 0.

lessons.title: The quadratic formula (Higher)
objectives: State and use the quadratic formula
Give answers to a stated degree of accuracy
Use the discriminant to say how many roots there are

keywords.def: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a, which solves ax² + bx + c = 0
the expression b² − 4ac under the square root
the number in front of a letter

starter: Evaluate b² − 4ac for a = 1, b = 3, c = −5.

teach.heading: The formula
teach.note: Write the formula in a box. Say it aloud as a rhythm. Identify a, b and c with their signs first. The ± gives two solutions.

teach.heading: Example 2 with a > 1
teach.note: Here −b = −(−5) = +5. Misconceptions: dividing by 2 not 2a, or only the square root by 2a. Use brackets on the calculator for the numerator and denominator.

teach.heading: The discriminant
teach.note: Example: x² + 2x + 5: 4 − 20 = −16 < 0 so no real solutions. The graph does not cross the x-axis. Ask: what does x² − 6x + 9 give? 36 − 36 = 0: one root, x = 3.

teach.heading: Checking
bullets: Substitute answers into the original equation.
teach.note: 1.19² = 1.4161; 3 × 1.19 = 3.57; total 1.4161 + 3.57 − 5 = −0.0139, close to 0 because the solution is rounded. Show how storing the unrounded value on a calculator gives a better check.

practice: Solve x² + 6x + 2 = 0 giving 2 decimal places.
Solve 3x² − 6x + 2 = 0 giving 2 decimal places.
How many roots does x² + 4x + 7 = 0 have?
independent: Solve x² + 5x + 3 = 0 to 2 d.p.
Solve 2x² + 3x − 7 = 0 to 2 d.p.
Write a quadratic equation with exactly one root and solve it with the formula.
exit: State the quadratic formula.
Use it to solve x² − 4x − 3 = 0 to 2 d.p.
lessons.homework: Solve four quadratics using the formula and check with a calculator.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-labelled a, b, c boxes. Stretch: show that the sum of the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0 is −b/a.

lessons.title: Pythagoras' theorem
objectives: Identify the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle
Calculate the hypotenuse or a shorter side using Pythagoras
Test whether a triangle is right-angled

keywords.def: the longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle
in a right-angled triangle, a² + b² = c² where c is the hypotenuse
the number that multiplies by itself to give a given number

starter: Which side of a right-angled triangle is the longest?

teach.heading: The theorem
bullets: Right-angled triangle with sides a, b and hypotenuse c.
The squares on the two shorter sides add to the square on the hypotenuse.
teach.note: Show a diagram with squares drawn on the sides of a 3-4-5 triangle: 9 + 16 = 25. Label the hypotenuse first every time. Ask: why can the theorem only be used in right-angled triangles?

teach.heading: Finding the hypotenuse
bullets: Sides 7 and 9: c² = 130, so c = 11.4 (1 d.p.).
teach.note: Add the squares, then square root. Check the hypotenuse is the longest side: 11.4 > 9 ✓. √130 = 11.40175..., giving 11.4 to 1 d.p.

teach.heading: Finding a shorter side
bullets: Subtract when finding a shorter side.
teach.note: Misconception: always adding. Sense check: the shorter side must be smaller than the hypotenuse. Second example: hypotenuse 15, side 9: 225 − 81 = 144, so the other side is 12.

teach.heading: Pythagorean triples
teach.note: To test for a right angle, check if a² + b² = c² for the longest side c. Example: 8, 9, 12 gives 64 + 81 = 145 but 12² = 144, so not a right angle (close, but not equal).

teach.heading: Rounding and accuracy
bullets: Leave answers as surds only if asked.
Otherwise round to a sensible accuracy.
teach.note: Encourage storing unrounded values on the calculator. Link: Islamic architecture uses right-angled constructions; ancient builders used knotted ropes with 3-4-5 lengths to make right angles.

practice: Find the hypotenuse for sides 5 cm and 12 cm.
Find the missing side: hypotenuse 17 cm, one side 8 cm.
Is a triangle with sides 9, 12, 15 right-angled?
independent: Find c for a = 7, b = 9 to 1 d.p.
Find the other side: hypotenuse 20 cm, one side 16 cm.
A rectangular screen is 24 cm by 18 cm. Find the diagonal.
exit: Find the hypotenuse of a triangle with sides 9 cm and 12 cm.
Find the missing side: hypotenuse 10 cm, one side 6 cm.
lessons.homework: Find three right-angled triangles in your home and use Pythagoras to check them.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: diagrams with the hypotenuse already coloured. Stretch: find a Pythagorean triple where the hypotenuse is 41.

lessons.title: Pythagoras in context and in 3D
objectives: Use Pythagoras to find the distance between two points
Solve problems with isosceles triangles and ladders
Apply Pythagoras in three dimensions

keywords.def: a pair of numbers (x, y) that give the position of a point
a line joining two non-adjacent vertices
a triangle with two equal sides

starter: Find the hypotenuse for sides 5 and 12.
Find the length of the line from (1, 2) to (1, 8).
Draw a right-angled triangle on a line.

teach.heading: Distance between points
teach.note: Draw the coordinate grid and make a right-angled triangle by going across and up. The distance is the hypotenuse. Ask: what would we do if the points were (−2, 3) and (4, −1)? Horizontal 6, vertical 4, distance √52 ≈ 7.21.

teach.heading: Isosceles triangles
bullets: Drop a perpendicular height: splits the base into 5 and 5.
teach.note: The perpendicular bisector makes two right-angled triangles. Area is ½ × 10 × 12 = 60 cm². Ask pupils to draw the triangle before calculating.

teach.heading: Ladders and ramps
bullets: A 5 m ladder has its foot 1.5 m from a wall.
teach.note: Make a sketch with the wall, ground and ladder. The ladder is the hypotenuse. Check: 4.77² + 1.5² = 22.75 + 2.25 = 25 ✓. Discuss ladder safety: the foot should be about one quarter of the height from the wall.

teach.heading: Diagonal of a rectangle
teach.note: Both 8-15-17 and 5-12-13 are common exam triples. Ask: why must the diagonal of a rectangle always be longer than either side?

teach.heading: Pythagoras in 3D
bullets: Cuboid 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm.
teach.note: Use two steps: first find the diagonal across the base, then use it with the height. Alternatively d² = a² + b² + c² = 9 + 16 + 144 = 169. Use a box to model.

practice: Find the distance between (0, 0) and (5, 12).
An isosceles triangle has equal sides 10 cm and base 12 cm. Find its height.
A ladder 6 m long reaches 5.5 m up a wall. How far from the wall is its foot?
independent: Find the distance between (−2, 3) and (4, −1) to 2 d.p.
A rectangle has diagonal 26 cm and one side 10 cm. Find the other side and the area.
A box is 6 cm by 8 cm by 24 cm. Find the longest straight line that fits inside.
exit: Find the distance between (1, 1) and (7, 9).
A 4 m ladder has its foot 1 m from a wall. How high does it reach (2 d.p.)?
lessons.homework: Find the length of the diagonal of your phone or tablet screen from its width and height and compare with the advertised size.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-drawn right-angled triangles on the coordinate grid. Stretch: show that the points (1, 1), (4, 5) and (8, 2) form an isosceles right-angled triangle.

lessons.title: Trigonometry: finding sides
objectives: Label the sides of a right-angled triangle as opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse
Choose between sin, cos and tan
Calculate a missing side

keywords.def: the side across from the angle being used
the side next to the angle being used, that is not the hypotenuse
ratios of sides in a right-angled triangle

starter: Find the hypotenuse for sides 6 and 8.

teach.heading: Labelling sides
bullets: Adjacent: next to the chosen angle.
teach.note: Opposite and adjacent change with the angle chosen; the hypotenuse never changes. Label three triangles on the board with different angles. Make sure the calculator is in degree mode (DEG).

teach.heading: SOH CAH TOA
teach.note: Use the mnemonic SOH CAH TOA. Decide which two sides are involved (one known, one wanted) and pick the ratio that uses exactly those sides.

teach.heading: Finding the opposite
teach.note: Multiply when the unknown is on top. Sense check: the opposite side is shorter than the hypotenuse ✓. Second example: tan 28° = O ÷ 9.5, so O = 9.5 × tan 28° = 5.05 cm.

teach.heading: Finding the adjacent
teach.note: The adjacent is also shorter than the hypotenuse. Ask pupils which ratio they would use if they knew the opposite and wanted the adjacent (tan).

teach.heading: Finding the hypotenuse
teach.note: When the unknown is on the bottom, divide. Common error: multiplying and getting 4.5 cm, which is smaller than the opposite side, an impossible answer. Always check the hypotenuse is the longest side.

practice: Find the opposite: angle 35°, hypotenuse 12 cm.
Find the adjacent: angle 50°, hypotenuse 8 cm.
Find the opposite: angle 28°, adjacent 9.5 cm.
independent: Find x if the angle is 32° and the adjacent side is 20 cm, opposite side x.
Find the hypotenuse: angle 25°, adjacent side 15 cm.
A ramp rises at 12° and is 5 m long. Find the vertical height.
exit: Find the opposite side: angle 40°, hypotenuse 10 cm.
Find the hypotenuse: angle 30°, opposite side 6 cm.
lessons.homework: Draw three right-angled triangles with different angles and use trigonometry to calculate a side, then measure to check.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: laminated SOH CAH TOA cards and a labelled-triangle template. Stretch: find x given tan 52° = x ÷ 8 and hence the hypotenuse.

lessons.title: Trigonometry: finding angles
objectives: Use inverse trigonometric functions to find angles
Solve angle of elevation problems
Choose between Pythagoras and trigonometry

keywords.def: undoes another function, such as sin⁻¹ undoing sin
the angle above the horizontal when looking up at an object
the angle below the horizontal when looking down

starter: Label the sides: opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse.

teach.heading: Inverse functions
bullets: If sin θ = 0.5, then θ = sin⁻¹(0.5) = 30°.
Check the calculator is in degree mode.
teach.note: Show how to use sin⁻¹ on the calculator. Check that sin 30° = 0.5 first, then reverse it. Ask pupils to verify their calculator mode with sin 30.

teach.heading: Finding an angle with sin
teach.note: Choose the ratio from the two sides known. Check sensible: since 5/8 is greater than 1/2, the angle is greater than 30° ✓.

teach.heading: Finding an angle with cos and tan
teach.note: Show both examples fully. Ask pupils how to decide which ratio to use: look at the labels of the two known sides. Remind them not to round before the inverse step.

teach.heading: Angle of elevation
teach.note: Draw the triangle with the ground horizontal. The angle of elevation is measured from the horizontal at the observer. A sketch is essential. Ask: how does the angle change if the observer moves closer?

teach.heading: Choosing a method
bullets: Two sides, need a side: Pythagoras.
teach.note: Give three mixed problems and ask pupils to choose the method before calculating. Check: if the angle is acute and the answer is more than 90°, an error has occurred.

practice: Find θ if sin θ = 0.8 (1 d.p.).
Find θ: opposite 7, adjacent 9.
Find θ: adjacent 4.5, hypotenuse 6.
independent: A ladder 6 m long has its foot 2 m from a wall. Find the angle with the ground.
A tree is 9 m high. From a point 15 m from its base, find the angle of elevation.
In a right-angled triangle the sides are 5, 12 and 13. Find the smallest angle.
exit: Find the angle θ where tan θ = 3/5.
A 10 m slope rises 3 m. Find the angle of the slope.
lessons.homework: Measure a height using a protractor, a tape measure and trigonometry, or complete the worksheet on angles of elevation.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: step list for calculator use. Stretch: find angles when two sides are given as surds.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Simultaneous equations, graphs and inequalities
lessons.title: Simultaneous linear equations
objectives: Solve simultaneous equations by elimination
Multiply one or both equations to match coefficients
Form and solve simultaneous equations from context

keywords.def: two or more equations that are true at the same time
adding or subtracting equations to remove one unknown
the number multiplying a letter

starter: Write an expression for the cost of 3 pens at p pence each.

teach.heading: Why elimination?
bullets: Make the coefficients of one letter equal.
Add or subtract to remove it.
teach.note: Explain that one equation x + y = 10 has many solutions, but two equations pin down exactly one pair. Rule: same signs subtract, different signs add (SSS: same signs subtract).

teach.heading: Subtracting
teach.note: Both equations have +2y, the same sign, so subtract. Check in both equations: 12 + 4 = 16 ✓ and 4 + 4 = 8 ✓. Insist on checking in the equation not used for substitution.

teach.heading: Adding
teach.note: The y terms have opposite signs (+3y and −3y), so add. Check: 15 − 6 = 9 ✓. Misconception: subtracting when the signs are different and getting 6y.

teach.heading: Multiplying first
teach.note: Multiply the whole equation, not just one term. Alternative route: eliminate y by multiplying by 5 and 2. Check: 3 + 4 = 7 ✓ and 2 + 10 = 12 ✓.

teach.heading: Context
bullets: Subtract: 2s = 4, so a samosa is £2 and a drink £1.75.
teach.note: Define the unknowns first (s and d). Check: 3 × 2 + 2 × 1.75 = 6 + 3.5 = 9.50 ✓ and 2 + 3.50 = 5.50 ✓. Link: honesty and fairness in trade.

practice: Solve x + y = 10 and x − y = 4.
Solve 4x + y = 19 and 2x + y = 11.
Solve 3x + 2y = 13 and 4x − 5y = 2.
independent: Solve 5x + 2y = 24 and 3x − 2y = 8.
Solve 2x + 3y = 8 and 3x + 2y = 7.
Two adult tickets and three child tickets cost £31. One adult and two child tickets cost £18. Find each price.
exit: Solve x + y = 9 and x − y = 3.
Solve 2x + y = 11 and x + y = 7.
lessons.homework: Create two simultaneous equation puzzles of your own, solve them and check the answers.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: colour-coded method card with SSS rule. Stretch: solve y = 2x − 1 and 3x + 2y = 12 by substitution.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Simultaneous equations, graphs and inequalities
lessons.title: Straight-line graphs: y = mx + c
objectives: Find the gradient and y-intercept of a line from its equation
Calculate gradient from two points
Find parallel lines

keywords.def: a measure of the steepness of a line: change in y divided by change in x
the point where the line crosses the y-axis
lines with the same gradient that never meet

teach.heading: y = mx + c
bullets: y = 2x + 1 has gradient 2 and crosses the y-axis at (0, 1).
teach.note: Draw y = 2x + 1: table of values x = 0, 1, 2, 3 gives y = 1, 3, 5, 7. Positive gradient goes up to the right. Ask: what does y = −x + 4 look like?

teach.heading: Calculating gradient
bullets: Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x.
Draw a right-angled triangle on the line.
teach.note: Take care with direction: subtract in the same order for both coordinates. Example with negative gradient: (2, 9) to (6, 1): change in y = −8, change in x = 4, gradient −2.

teach.heading: Finding the equation
teach.note: Check with the other point: 2 × 5 + 1 = 11 ✓. Pupils must always check using the second point.

teach.heading: Rearranging to y = mx + c
teach.note: Misconception: 2y = 6x + 4 gives y = 6x + 2 (dividing only one term). Practise reading gradient and intercept from rearranged forms.

teach.heading: Parallel lines
teach.note: Check: 3 × 2 + 3 = 9 ✓. Which of y = 2x + 5, 4x − 2y = 3 and y = 3 − 2x are parallel? The first two (4x − 2y = 3 gives y = 2x − 1.5).

practice: Find the gradient between (0, 2) and (4, 10).
Write 2y = 8x − 6 in the form y = mx + c.
Find the equation of the line with gradient 4 through (0, −3).
independent: Find the equation of the line through (2, 7) and (6, 15).
Find the equation of the line parallel to y = 5x − 1 through (1, 9).
Which of y = 2x + 5, 4x − 2y = 3 and y = 3 − 2x are parallel?
exit: State the gradient and intercept of y = −3x + 4.
Find the equation of the line through (0, 1) and (3, 7).
lessons.homework: Sketch five lines of the form y = mx + c, labelling their gradient and intercept.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: gradient triangles on squared paper. Stretch: find where y = 2x + 1 meets y = −x + 7.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Simultaneous equations, graphs and inequalities
lessons.title: Equation of a line and perpendicular lines (Higher)
objectives: Find the equation of a line through two points
Find the gradient of a perpendicular line
Find the equation of a perpendicular line through a point

keywords.def: meeting at a right angle
flip the fraction and change the sign
an equation whose graph is a straight line

starter: Write the reciprocal of 2 and of −3.
Make y the subject of 2y + x = 6.

teach.heading: Two points
teach.note: Check with the second point: −3 × 4 + 10 = −2 ✓. A line sketch helps to see a negative gradient going down to the right.

teach.heading: Perpendicular gradients
bullets: The perpendicular to gradient 2 has gradient −1/2.
teach.note: Show on squared paper by rotating a gradient triangle 90°: 2 up, 1 across becomes 1 up, 2 back. Examples: 3 becomes −1/3; −4 becomes 1/4; 2/5 becomes −5/2.

teach.heading: Equation of a perpendicular line
teach.note: Check that the point (4, 1) lies on the line: −½ × 4 + 3 = 1 ✓. The y-intercept of the original is not used.

teach.heading: Testing perpendicular
teach.note: Always rearrange into y = mx + c first. Ask: are y = 3x and y = −3x perpendicular? (No: the product is −9.) Mixed practice helps distinguish parallel from perpendicular.

teach.heading: Reading a problem
teach.note: Check with (2, 7): 4 + 3 = 7 ✓. Link to perpendicular: the perpendicular through (−2, −1) has gradient −1/2 and equation y = −½x − 2.

practice: Find the equation of the line through (1, 3) and (3, 7).
State the gradient of a line perpendicular to y = 4x − 1.
Are y = ½x − 4 and y = −2x + 5 perpendicular?
independent: Find the line perpendicular to y = ½x − 4 through (0, 5).
Find the line perpendicular to y = 3x + 1 through (6, 1).
Show that the line through (0, 2) and (4, 4) is perpendicular to the line through (1, 5) and (2, 3).
exit: Find the gradient of a line perpendicular to y = −5x + 2.
Find the equation of the line through (0, 4) with gradient 3.
lessons.homework: Make a one-page summary of parallel and perpendicular line rules with two worked examples.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: step prompts and gradient triangles. Stretch: find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of the line segment from (1, 2) to (5, 6).

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Simultaneous equations, graphs and inequalities
lessons.title: Solving linear inequalities
objectives: Solve linear inequalities
Represent solutions on a number line
List the integers satisfying an inequality

keywords.def: a statement comparing two values using <, >, ≤ or ≥
a whole number, positive, negative or zero
all the values that make an inequality true

starter: Write 'x is at least 3' using a symbol.

teach.heading: Inequality symbols
bullets: ≤ less than or equal; ≥ greater than or equal.
Open circle: not included. Closed circle: included.
teach.note: Practise reading symbols aloud. Number line: x > 5 has an open circle at 5 and an arrow right; x ≤ 5 has a filled circle at 5 and an arrow left.

teach.heading: Solving like equations
teach.note: Use the same steps as equations. Test a value: x = 6 gives 14 > 11 ✓ while x = 5 gives 11 which is not greater. 2x + 7 ≤ 1 gives 2x ≤ −6, so x ≤ −3.

teach.heading: Negative coefficient
bullets: Divide by −2 and reverse the sign.
teach.note: Show why: −2 < 3 but 2 > −3 when multiplied by −1. Alternatively add 2x to both sides: 0 ≤ 6 + 2x, so x ≥ −3. Test x = 0: 0 ≤ 6 ✓.

teach.heading: Double inequalities
teach.note: Do the same to all three parts. Integers: −1, 0, 1, 2, 3. Ask why −1.5 is not an integer and why 4 is excluded.

teach.heading: Context
teach.note: Interpret the answer in context: only whole tickets can be bought, so round down. Another: if each box holds 12 and we need to hold at least 100 items: 12n ≥ 100 gives n ≥ 8.33, so at least 9 boxes.

practice: Solve 5x − 3 ≤ 17.
Solve 4 − 3x < 19.
List the integers with −2 < x ≤ 2.
independent: Solve 7 < 2x + 1 ≤ 15 and list the integers.
Solve 3(x − 2) ≥ 9 and show it on a number line.
A taxi costs £3 plus £2 per mile. Yusuf has £25. Write and solve an inequality for the number of miles.
exit: Solve 3x + 2 > 14.
Solve −4x ≥ 20.
lessons.homework: Write five inequalities, solve them, draw the number lines and test one value for each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: number line templates with open and closed circle examples. Stretch: solve x² < 16.

lessons.title: Probability: relative frequency, expected outcomes and sample spaces
objectives: Calculate theoretical probability and relative frequency
Estimate how many times an outcome is expected
Use sample space diagrams to find probabilities

keywords.def: the number of times an outcome happens divided by the number of trials
the list or table of all possible outcomes
probability multiplied by the number of trials

starter: Bismillah. What is the probability of rolling a 4 on a fair dice?
Write 0.35 as a fraction and a percentage.
If P(rain) = 0.3, what is P(no rain)?

teach.heading: Probability basics
bullets: The probabilities of all outcomes add to 1.
teach.note: Use a fair dice as the standard example. Ask pupils to place events on a probability line: impossible 0, evens 0.5, certain 1. Misconception: 'the chances are 50:50 because it either happens or does not'.

teach.heading: Relative frequency
bullets: A dice is rolled 60 times; 6 appears 18 times.
A fair dice gives 1/6 ≈ 0.167, so this dice may be biased.
teach.note: More trials give a better estimate of the true probability. 60 trials is small. Ask: how could we improve our estimate? (Roll many more times.)

teach.heading: Expected outcomes
bullets: Expected number = probability × number of trials.
teach.note: Expected is an average, not a guarantee. A fair coin tossed 100 times is expected to give 50 heads but 47 or 54 would not be surprising.

teach.heading: Sample space for two dice
bullets: Two dice have 36 equally likely outcomes.
Sum of at least 10 appears 6 times: P = 1/6.

teach.heading: Systematic listing
bullets: Two coins: HH, HT, TH, TT.
teach.note: HT and TH are different outcomes. Misconception: pupils think the three outcomes 'two heads, two tails, one of each' are equally likely. They are not.

practice: A spinner lands on red 18 times in 60 spins. Find the relative frequency of red.
P(rain on a given day) = 0.35. How many wet days expected in 120 days?
Find the probability of a total of 8 with two dice.
independent: A spinner has red 18 times, blue 30 times, green 12 times in 60 spins. Find each relative frequency and check they add to 1.
Predict how many blues in 150 spins.
Two spinners each have 1, 2, 3. Draw a sample space and find P(total 4).
exit: P(a bus is late) = 0.15. How many late buses expected in 200 journeys?
Two coins are tossed. Find P(two tails).
lessons.homework: Roll two dice 36 times and compare your relative frequencies with the theoretical probabilities.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-drawn sample space grids. Stretch: find P(product is even) using a 6 by 6 table.

lessons.title: Tree diagrams: independent events
objectives: Draw tree diagrams for two or more independent events
Multiply along branches and add between outcomes
Find probabilities of 'at least one'

keywords.def: events where one outcome does not affect the other
a diagram of branches showing all outcomes and their probabilities
an item is put back before the next pick

starter: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue counters. Find P(red).

teach.heading: Branches
bullets: Each branch shows an outcome and its probability.
Branches from one point add to 1.
A bag has 4 red and 6 blue counters; one is taken and replaced.
teach.note: Draw the first column with R (0.4) and B (0.6), and the second column identical because the counter is replaced. Check each pair adds to 1.

teach.heading: The multiplication rule
teach.note: Explain: 0.4 of the time we get red first, and then 0.4 of those times red second. List all four outcomes: RR 0.16, RB 0.24, BR 0.24, BB 0.36. They add to 1 ✓.

teach.heading: The addition rule
teach.note: 'One of each' can be RB or BR, so add. Always check the total is 1. Ask: why is it wrong to multiply 0.4 × 0.6 only once for this case?

teach.heading: At least one
bullets: P(at least one red) = 1 − P(no red).
teach.note: Complement method: 'at least one' is everything except 'none'. Verify: 0.16 + 0.48 = 0.64 ✓. This approach is much faster for three or more events.

teach.heading: A context
teach.note: The events are independent if the days are not affected by each other. Then P(at least one late) = 1 − 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.36 ✓ (0.04 + 0.32).

practice: A fair coin is tossed twice. Draw a tree and find P(two heads).
P(red) = 0.3 on a spinner. It is spun twice. Find P(red, then not red).
Find P(at least one red) in two spins.
independent: P(rain) = 0.3 on Monday and Tuesday. Find P(rain both days) and P(no rain either day).
A spinner has P(red) = 0.3. It is spun twice. Find P(exactly one red).
A coin is tossed three times. Find P(three heads) and P(at least one head).
exit: P(pass) = 0.7 for each of two tests. Find P(pass both).
Find P(pass exactly one).
lessons.homework: Draw a tree diagram for a real-life situation with two independent events and calculate all four probabilities.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: tree diagram templates with branch labels. Stretch: three spins with P(red) = 0.3: find P(at least one red).

lessons.title: Tree diagrams: dependent events
objectives: Recognise when events are dependent
Adjust probabilities when items are not replaced
Solve problems involving two picks without replacement

keywords.def: events where the first outcome changes the probability of the second
an item is kept out before the next pick
the probability of an event given that another has happened

starter: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue counters. Find P(blue).

teach.heading: What changes?
bullets: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue counters.
One is taken and not replaced.
The second pick is from 7 counters.
teach.note: Contrast with replacement: the second column of the tree changes. If red was taken first, there are 4 red and 3 blue left (4/7 and 3/7).

teach.heading: Building the tree
teach.note: Check that each pair of branches adds to 1. Ask pupils to explain each fraction in words. Misconception: keeping 5/8 and 3/8 on the second pick.

teach.heading: Chocolates
bullets: 4 dark and 2 milk chocolates; two eaten.

teach.heading: Conditional probability (Higher)
bullets: Given the first is red, P(second red) = 4/7.
Read from the second set of branches.
teach.note: The phrase 'given that' tells us the first event has already happened. Ask: how does P(second red | first red) differ from P(second red)? The first is 4/7; the second, over all cases, is 5/8 (by symmetry).

practice: A bag has 7 counters: 3 green, 4 yellow. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(both green).
Find P(both yellow).
Find P(different colours).
independent: A box has 6 red and 4 green sweets. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(both red) and P(both green).
Find P(at least one red).
A bag has 4 black and 5 white socks. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(same colour).
exit: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(both red).
Find P(one red and one blue).
lessons.homework: Draw a tree diagram for taking two counters without replacement from a bag you choose, and calculate all outcomes.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: tree diagram templates with first-pick fractions filled in. Stretch: three counters taken without replacement from 5 red and 3 blue: find P(all red).

lessons.title: Venn diagrams and set notation
objectives: Use set notation: union, intersection and complement
Complete Venn diagrams from given information
Calculate probabilities, including conditional, from Venn diagrams

keywords.def: all elements in A, in B, or in both
only the elements in both A and B
all elements not in A

starter: List the factors of 12 and of 18.
Which numbers are in both lists?

teach.heading: Set notation
bullets: A ∪ B: in A or B or both.
A ∩ B: in both A and B.
teach.note: Draw a Venn diagram with two overlapping circles inside a rectangle. Shade each region as you introduce the notation. Example: A = {2, 4, 6, 8}, B = {3, 6, 9}; A ∩ B = {6}; A ∪ B = {2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9}.

teach.heading: Filling a Venn diagram
teach.note: Always start with the overlap, then subtract. Neither = 40 − (14 + 8 + 10) = 40 − 32 = 8. Check that all regions add to 40 ✓.

teach.heading: Reading a Venn diagram
teach.note: n(A) means the number of elements in A. Ask pupils to describe in words what F′ is (pupils who do not play football) and why n(F′) = 18 (10 cricket-only plus 8 neither).

teach.heading: Probabilities
teach.note: Divide the region count by the total (40). Check complementary: P(F ∪ C) + P(neither) = 4/5 + 1/5 = 1 ✓.

teach.heading: Conditional (Higher)
bullets: P(football | cricket): restrict to the cricket circle.
teach.note: 'Given' restricts the denominator to the given set. The two conditional probabilities are different because the circles have different sizes. Common error: dividing by 40.

practice: A = {2, 4, 6, 8} and B = {3, 6, 9}. Find A ∪ B and A ∩ B.
30 pupils: 15 play A, 12 play B, 5 play both. How many play neither?
In the same group find P(A and B).
independent: 50 pupils: 28 study Arabic, 20 study French, 6 study both. Draw and complete a Venn diagram.
Find P(Arabic only) and P(neither).
Higher: find P(Arabic | French).
exit: Describe A ∩ B′ in words.
In a Venn diagram, 10 are in A only, 5 in both, 7 in B only, 8 in neither. Find P(A).
lessons.homework: Survey 20 people about two drinks they like and draw a Venn diagram of the results.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: Venn templates with regions labelled. Stretch: three-set Venn diagram problem with 60 pupils.
